title: Michael Johnson accused of fraud over $500k ‘secret’ payment from Grand Slam Track
content:
Four-time U.S. Olympic gold medalist Michael Johnson has been accused of fraud after his Grand Slam Track league “secretly” transferred $500,000 to him at a time when he allegedly knew that there were insufficient funds to pay competing athletes in his start-up competition.

The allegation has been made by a group of GST vendors, who on Monday requested permission from a bankruptcy court to also sue the management and board members of GST, as well as its lead investor, the Bill Ackman-backed fund Winners Alliance, for no less than $25 million.

In the new legal filing, published in the United States Bankruptcy Court for the District of Delaware, the former sprinter Johnson is accused of having taken the $500,000 payment without approval from the GST board. The payment took place on June 4, 2025, eight days before GST cancelled its final meet, scheduled for Los Angeles.

At the time of the payment, athletes and vendors providing services to the league had not been informed of GST’s perilous financial predicament, with the opening three meets having taken place in Kingston, Jamaica, Miami and Philadelphia.

The filings record an investigation made by a representative group of creditors attempting to claw back $12.9 million owed to them by GST. In their filing, they say that GST lost $37.2 million in the first six months of 2025, and was plunged into crisis when the investment fund Eldridge, chaired by Chelsea part-owner Todd Boehly, elected not to press on with a proposed investment following an underwhelming opening meet in Jamaica.

The filing also says that Winners Alliance’s initial investment was in fact only $13 million, as first reported by The Athletic in August, and that GST did not have access to the $30 million it claimed it had secured upon announcing its launch in June 2024. Indeed, the filing even claims that by the start of 2025, GST had only $5.5 million in cash, and GST’s “own internal projections showed this amount was insufficient to even get through a single track meet even if GST hit its revenue target.”

GST fell wildly short of its $14.5 million revenue projection for 2025, bringing in only $1.8 million across its three events. It has previously submitted an extensive record of its assets and liabilities, which revealed total debts of $40.68 million compared to $831,385 in assets.

The complaint against Johnson relates to the $500,000 payment made to him in June. Previous filings have recorded that Johnson put $2.25 million into the business on May 23, 2025, just one week before the third event in Philadelphia — an event which The Athletic has reported GST considered cancelling  — before recovering $500,000 on June 4.

Johnson is one of the only parties to have recovered some of what he put in. In January, GST did not comment when asked by The Athletic if the $500,000 repayment to Johnson required or received GST board approval.

The Athletic contacted Johnson for comment on Tuesday afternoon. A spokesperson for GST later responded on his behalf to say: “We will not be drawn into a battle of allegations or misrepresentations.  The Chapter 11 process is completely transparent.  We support full transparency.  We will stay focused, disciplined, and steadfast in the process.

“GST staff, supporters, and its principals, have made, and continue to make, both before and after filing, extraordinary personal efforts to make this situation right for everyone involved.”

The creditor committee filing alleges: “Approximately one week before announcing the June 10 cancellation of its Los Angeles event, Mr. Johnson initiated a payment of $500,000 purportedly on account of an unsecured note. There are no Board minutes which reflect authorization of this insider avoidable transfer. Shockingly, Mr. Johnson elected to secretly prefer himself over the athletes and other, non-insider creditors, while at the same time feigning to the public that he was selflessly looking to advance the interests of the athletes.”

The group of creditors are seeking to block a bankruptcy plan by GST, supported by Winners Alliance, which would pay athletes 85 per cent of the monies still owed, while only paying vendors 1.5 per cent. They argue this is because GST is seeking to prioritize its relationship with athletes to facilitate a possible path forward for the project and protect the reputation of Johnson and his lead investor, Winners Alliance, whose board is chaired by hedge fund manager Ackman. Winners’ stated mission is to “equip world-class athlete groups with the resources needed to protect and maximize their collective rights.”

The creditors committee who have made the filing is comprised of production company Momentum-CHP Partnership, graphics firm Girraphic Park, and GST ex-PR firm SRK Strategies. The three creditors are collectively owed more than $4 million.

The vendors have turned their ire on the leaders of GST, rather than the bankrupt league itself, with a proposed lawsuit seeking action against Winners Alliance, Johnson, GST chief operating officer Steve Gera, billionaire board member Robert Smith, and Winners Alliance executives Vivek Khanna, Ahmad Nassar and Eric Winston.

The vendors accuse Winners of “prioritizing its equity investment over prudent financial management” and “actively encouraging (GST) to worsen its financial position and deepen its insolvency on the back of its creditors who were unaware of the Debtor’s financial difficulty.” The accusation has been denied by Winners Alliance.

Last week, the creditors committee accused Winners of “orchestrating” every step of GST since before the league was even incorporated and of turning a “blind eye” as the league plunged toward bankruptcy.

As part of the bankruptcy plan, Winners would provide the $6 million to pay athletes, but it would leave vendors severely out of pocket. The list of creditors owed includes major companies, public institutions and brands. For example, the W Hotel in Los Angeles is owed around $350,000, and there is a $339,000 credit-card balance owed to American Express. The City of Miramar in Florida is also owed more than $77,000, likely for the use of its Ansin Sports Complex to stage the Miami meet. More than $135,000 is owed to Penn Athletics, which hosted the third meet at Franklin Field in Philadelphia.

Winners Alliance filed its own defense on Tuesday, in which the group categorically denied that it ran GST and described the objections of the creditors committee as “fundamentally false.”

It continued: “The Committee resorts to disparaging rhetoric and a series of inflammatory allegations … The Committee’s transparent tactic to extort additional funds from WA (Winners Alliance) through a reputational smear campaign should not be countenanced. The Committee’s opposition is full of unsubstantiated claims.

“Most of the Committee’s theories rests on a single premise: that WA exercised ‘control’ over GST from before its inception. That premise is the foundation for a litany of claims the Committee wishes it could prove. It is also demonstrably false. And, the Committee knows it is untrue. The undisputed facts show that at all times, WA was a minority shareholder in GST and held a minority of GST’s board seats. GST’s corporate governance documents, which the Committee has had access to, make this unambiguously clear.

“WA also did not exercise operational control over the Debtor. GST employees, not WA, managed the Debtor’s operations. WA did not select GST’s vendors. WA did not negotiate athlete contracts. WA did not choose event venues or determine event logistics. WA did not hire or fire GST employees. WA did not run GST’s fundraising process — that was led by GST’s CEO and President through PJT Partners, GST’s investment bankers.

“WA did not source or manage the Eldridge Industries investment that was expected to close in April 2025. WA did not source or manage the subsequent funding discussions with GST board member Robert Smith’s network or Sundial Media Group (who were selected by, and communicated with, Michael Johnson and were previously unknown to WA).

“At every stage, GST’s management made operational decisions, and WA — as a minority shareholder with a minority of board seats — had neither the authority nor the ability to override them. The Committee’s assertion that WA ‘orchestrated the Debtor’s every step’ is not merely unsupported — it is contradicted by every corporate governance document the Committee has in its possession.”

In its defense, GST said the filing by the creditors committee “reeks of desperation for any reason, however far-fetched, to attempt to derail (GST’s) confirmation efforts” and is “best-characterized as an ill-conceived proposal to destroy the Debtor’s future prospects.”
